docs.title: fiber-guard
docs.text:
fiber-guard is the official Fiber v3 adapter for guard-core-go, the Go port of the guard-core security engine. It wraps any Fiber app with the full engine pipeline: penetration detection, rate limiting, IP banning, and verdict responses.

All security logic lives in the engine; this package is a thin shim that translates fiber.Ctx into guardcore.Request, runs the engine, and writes the block verdict when one arrives.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
go get github.com/rennf93/fiber-guard github.com/rennf93/guard-core-go/v4@v4.1.0

Requires Go 1.25 or later and Fiber v3.5 or later.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
package main

import (
    "log"

    fiberlib "github.com/gofiber/fiber/v3"
    guardcore "github.com/rennf93/guard-core-go/v4/guardcore"
    guardfiber "github.com/rennf93/fiber-guard"
)

func main() {
    cfg := guardcore.DefaultSecurityConfig()
    engine, err := guardcore.NewEngine(cfg)
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    if err := engine.Initialize(); err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    defer func() { _ = engine.Close() }()

    guard, err := guardfiber.New(engine)
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }

    app := fiberlib.New()
    app.Use(guard)
    app.Get("/", func(c fiberlib.Ctx) error {
        return c.SendString("ok")
    })

    log.Fatal(app.Listen(":8080"))
}

docs.title: What the shim handles
docs.text:
• Client identity: RequestCtx().RemoteIP() from the fasthttp transport, with trusted-proxy resolution performed by the engine (SecurityConfig.TrustedProxies). Fiber's c.IP() is intentionally not used: with TrustProxy plus a ProxyHeader configured it resolves the client from proxy headers, and trusting proxy headers is policy the core owns.
  • Headers: first value per key, read from RequestCtx().Request.Header.All()
  • Body: fasthttp buffers the full body before the middleware runs, the engine sees only the first maxBodyBytes bytes, and the handler reads the full, untouched body straight from Fiber
  • Route IDs: read from the Fiber user context (see Usage)
  • Fail-closed: engine panics become 500 with a fixed, non-leaky message

See Configuration for engine tuning and the examples for runnable apps.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: The adapter has exactly two options (WithMaxBodyBytes, WithLogger); all security tuning is engine configuration. See the guard-core-go configuration reference for the full SecurityConfig surface.

docs.title: Minimal tuned setup
docs.text:
cfg := guardcore.DefaultSecurityConfig()
cfg.EnableRateLimiting = true
cfg.RateLimit = 30
cfg.RateLimitWindow = 60
cfg.EndpointRateLimits = map[string]guardcore.RateLimitEntry{
    "/rate/strict": {Requests: 1, Window: 10},
}
cfg.EnableIPBanning = true
cfg.AutoBanThreshold = 5
cfg.AutoBanDuration = 300
cfg.CustomErrorResponses = map[int]string{
    403: "Blocked by fiber-guard",
}

docs.title: Address headers
docs.text:
The Python engine skips ssrf scanning for address headers (host, x-forwarded-for, x-real-ip, ...) automatically. The Go engine does not apply that built-in exclusion yet, so mirror it explicitly when clients can send internal hostnames; the Fiber adapter forwards fasthttp's explicit Host header, so host must be in the set:

cfg.ExcludedDetectionHeaders = map[string]bool{
    "host": true, "origin": true, "via": true,
    "x-forwarded-for": true, "x-forwarded-host": true,
    "x-real-ip": true, "x-client-ip": true,
}

docs.title: Redis
docs.text:
Distributed bans and rate limits require Redis:

cfg.EnableRedis = true
cfg.RedisURL = os.Getenv("REDIS_URL") // e.g. redis://redis:6379
cfg.RedisPrefix = "fiber_guard:"

Without Redis the managers fall back to in-process state, which does not share across replicas.

docs.title: Body inspection
docs.text: WithMaxBodyBytes bounds what the detector sees. Bodies larger than the limit are still forwarded to your handler in full (fasthttp buffers the whole body before the middleware runs); only the inspected prefix is truncated. The default matches the engine's MaxBodyInspectBytes (262144).

docs.title: Trusted proxies
docs.text:
The adapter resolves the client from the fasthttp transport peer (RequestCtx().RemoteIP()), never from c.IP(): with TrustProxy plus a ProxyHeader configured, Fiber would resolve the client from proxy headers, and trusting proxy headers is policy the engine owns. When behind a reverse proxy, trust only the proxy hop so the engine resolves the real client IP from forwarded headers:

cfg.TrustedProxies = []string{"172.16.0.0/12", "10.0.0.0/8"}
cfg.TrustedProxyDepth = 1

docs.title: Constructor
docs.text:
func New(engine *guardcore.Engine, opts ...Option) (fiberlib.Handler, error)

New returns the Fiber middleware handler. It rejects a nil engine with an error; invalid option values are silently ignored so a bad flag can never weaken security.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Default Purpose WithMaxBodyBytes(int64) DefaultMaxBodyBytes (262144) Body prefix handed to the engine for inspection WithLogger(*log.Logger) none Receive fail-closed diagnostics (prefix guardcore fiber: ...) 
guard, err := guardfiber.New(engine,
    guardfiber.WithMaxBodyBytes(64*1024),
    guardfiber.WithLogger(log.New(os.Stderr, "", log.LstdFlags)),
)

docs.title: Route IDs
docs.text:
Per-route configuration lives in the engine's RouteRegistry. Attach a route ID to the Fiber user context before the guard runs by registering the ID middleware first with app.Use:

engine.Routes.Register("admin", func(rc *guardcore.RouteConfig) {
    rc.RequiredHeaders = guardcore.RequiredHeaders{
        {Name: "X-Admin-Token", Value: "secret"},
    }
})

routeIDs := map[string]string{"/admin/banned": "admin", "/admin/ban": "admin"}
app.Use(func(c fiberlib.Ctx) error {
    if routeID, ok := routeIDs[c.Path()]; ok {
        c.SetContext(guardfiber.WithRouteID(c.Context(), routeID))
    }
    return c.Next()
})
app.Use(guard)

Fiber v3 caveat: inside a use-registered middleware, c.Route() (and with it c.FullPath()) still points at the middleware's own route entry, because the router reassigns c.route for every matched tree entry as the chain executes. Match on the concrete request path (c.Path()) instead; parameterized routes need one map entry per concrete path.

docs.title: Verdicts
docs.text:
When the engine returns a block verdict, the middleware writes the verdict status code, headers, and body, and never calls c.Next():

Situation Status Body Banned IP 403 IP address banned Suspicious content 400 Suspicious activity detected Rate limit exceeded 429 Too many requests

Bodies can be overridden globally through SecurityConfig.CustomErrorResponses.

docs.title: Fail-closed behavior
docs.text: If the engine check panics, the middleware recovers, logs through the WithLogger sink, and responds 500 Security check failed rather than letting the request through.
